title: War Powers
short: Congress declares war and funds the military; the President commands it; Congress has declared war only eleven times in five wars, and the War Powers Resolution (1973) requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours and to end action within 60 days (plus 30) without its approval.
trouble: Students think every war was declared by Congress. Korea, Vietnam, the Gulf War and others were fought under resolutions, treaties or the President's authority without a declaration.

blocks.html: The Constitution splits war between the branches on purpose. Congress may "declare War," "raise and support Armies," "provide and maintain a Navy" and fund them (powers of Congress); the President is "Commander in Chief" (a formal power). Hamilton wrote that the President's command would amount to "nothing more than the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces, as first General and admiral of the Confederacy," by which he meant the Union (Federalist No. 69).

head: War
Declared
blocks.cap: All eleven declarations of war, in five wars (U.S. Senate).

blocks.html: Since 1942 Congress has declared no wars. Korea (1950) was fought under United Nations resolutions on the President's authority; Vietnam under the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964); the Gulf War (1991), Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2002) under authorizations for the use of military force passed by Congress. After Vietnam, Congress passed the War Powers Resolution (1973) over President Nixon's veto. It requires the President to report to Congress within 48 hours of sending forces into hostilities, and to end the action within 60 days (plus up to 30 more to withdraw safely) unless Congress declares war or authorizes it. Presidents of both parties have questioned whether it is constitutional, while usually filing the reports; Congress and scholars continue to argue over where the line between the two powers lies.

doc.title: From the War Powers Resolution (1973)
paras: Section 4 (in part): ...the president shall submit within 48 hours to the Speaker of the House of Representatives and to the President pro tempore of the Senate a report, in writing...

Section 5 (in part): Within sixty calendar days after a report is submitted or is required to be submitted..., the President shall terminate any use of United States Armed Forces with respect to which such report was submitted..., unless the Congress (1) has declared war or has enacted a specific authorization for such use of United States Armed Forces, (2) has extended by law such sixty-day period, or (3) is physically unable to meet as a result of an armed attack upon the United States.

marks.note: The clock for ending action without Congress's approval (plus up to 30 days to withdraw).

blocks.html: Congress declares war and funds the military; the President commands it. Congress has declared war only eleven times in five wars. The War Powers Resolution (1973) requires notice within 48 hours and an end to action within 60 days (plus 30) without Congress's approval.

blocks.title: Run the clock
blocks.q: A President sends forces into hostilities and reports to Congress on March 1. Congress neither declares war nor authorizes the action. About when must the action end under the War Powers Resolution?
steps: Sixty days after the report: about April 30.
Up to thirty more days are allowed for safe withdrawal: about May 30.
blocks.a: About 60 days after the report, plus up to 30 days to withdraw.

blocks.title: Declared or not?
blocks.q: Was the Korean War declared by Congress?
steps: Korea (1950) was fought under United Nations Security Council resolutions and the President's authority, without a declaration.

blocks.html: Thinking every war was declared by Congress. Korea, Vietnam, the Gulf War, Afghanistan, Iraq and many smaller actions were fought under resolutions, treaties or the President's own authority, without a declaration. Check: the last declaration of war was in 1942.
